verdict.plain: The triple lock raises all state pensions equally, which helps the poorest pensioners keep up with living costs, but the growing fiscal cost falls on working-age people who are now relatively less well-off than pensioners as a group — so it narrows one gap while widening another. Whether the net effect narrows or widens inequality overall depends on which gap you weight more.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether the fiscal cost is met by broad-based taxes (falling on all workers) or targeted measures would significantly alter the distributional verdict for working-age lower earners.

verdict.rationale: The triple lock is a flat-rate uplift to a flat-rate benefit, so in proportional terms all pensioners receive the same increase. For the poorest pensioners most dependent on the state pension, this does provide some protection against falling behind — yet the evidence undermines the poverty-reduction narrative: pensioner poverty has risen since 2011/12 despite the policy, and the average pension still falls well short of a minimum acceptable standard. On the intergenerational dimension, the picture is clearer and more adverse for O14: pensioners as a group have already reached income parity with working-age households after two decades of faster living standards growth, yet the triple lock continues to grow the share of national income flowing to that group. The growing fiscal cost — £12 billion a year above an earnings link already — creates pressure on taxes or other public services, with the burden landing disproportionately on working-age people who are, on average, no longer materially better off than pensioners. Critics including the Resolution Foundation and Intergenerational Foundation explicitly frame this as a transfer from younger, less affluent workers to older and in aggregate wealthier pensioners. The net distributional verdict across the whole income distribution is therefore mixed: there is a genuine, if limited, case that the floor under the poorest pensioners is somewhat higher than it would be otherwise (narrowing one gap), while the intergenerational and within-working-age distributional effects point in the opposite direction (widening another gap). The absence of evidence that the triple lock reduces pensioner poverty in practice keeps confidence at moderate and prevents a clear 'improves' verdict.

verifier.notes: All claims are well-grounded in the cited evidence. The E6 and E7 claims are Resolution Foundation figures — an institutional source, acceptable. E23 (Intergenerational Foundation) is an advocacy source but is correctly labelled as a critic's argument in projected tier, not used as sole basis for the verdict. The mixed direction is genuinely supported by claims pointing in both directions: narrowing effect for poorest pensioners (E9 shows floor exists) vs. widening intergenerational gap (E6, E23, E14). The counter-side has real claims behind it so false_balance does not apply. Tier integrity is sound — E4 is measurable (OBR/Commons Library historical fact by 2023/24), E14 is projected (IFS estimate) correctly labelled. No motive attribution or party identity language detected. Magnitude 'minor' and time_horizon 'long-term' are reasonable given the contested and slow-moving distributional effects. No n/a violations.

evidence.snippet: Support pensioners by protecting the triple lock so that pensions always rise in line with inflation, wages or 2.5% – whichever is highest.

The UK's State Pension Triple Lock policy commits to increasing the basic and new State Pension each year by the highest of three measures: inflation (as measured by the Consumer Price Index, CPI), average earnings growth, or 2.5%
This policy was introduced by the Coalition Government in 2011/12 to improve the value of the State Pension relative to prices and earnings
It has been applied every year since, with a temporary suspension in 2022/23 due to distorted earnings figures following the COVID-19 pandemic
*   By 2023/24, the cumulative effect meant the basic State Pension was nearly £800 a year higher than if it had been uprated by either earnings or CPI inflation alone since 2011/12
*   The full new State Pension, which was £185.15 a week in 2022/23, is projected to reach £241.30 a week (£12,548 a year) in 2026/27, representing a more than 30% increase in four years

*   The Resolution Foundation notes that pensioners have seen three times as much living standards growth as non-pensioners over the last two decades, with a typical pensioner household now having a similar income level to a typical working-age household

This think tank argues that the triple lock has been largely ineffective at reducing poverty, as pensioner poverty rates have risen by 2.3 percentage points in the 12 years following its introduction, compared to a 15.8 percentage point fall in the 15 years prior
However, **Age UK** expresses concerns, stating that many older people still struggle to afford a decent standard of living, with one in six pensioners living in relative poverty

They highlight that even with increases, the average annual State Pension (£9,500 after a 10.1% increase in April 2023) remains below the £12,800 per year required for a "minimum" lifestyle as defined by the Pensions and Lifetime Savings Association

*   **Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)**: The OBR has highlighted a "ratchet effect" where the triple lock increases State Pension rates and spending as a proportion of GDP over time, especially following economic shocks, because increases are never fully unwound
However, updated projections now suggest a much larger figure of £15.5 billion annually by 2029/30, nearly three times the original estimate
*   Spending on the State Pension is projected to rise by around £80 billion over the next 50 years, with over half of this increase attributed to the triple lock
*   State Pension spending currently accounts for 5% of GDP (£138 billion), and the OBR projects this could rise to 7.7% by the early 2070s

*   **Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS)**: The IFS estimates that the triple lock has increased annual government spending by £12 billion more in 2025-26 than if it had been uprated in line with average earnings since 2011

They also project that additional State Pension spending in 2050 could range between £5 billion and £40 billion a year in today's money compared to an earnings-only link, underscoring the policy's unpredictability and fiscal risk
*   **Resolution Foundation**: This think tank views the triple lock as "fiscally unsustainable" and "unpredictable"
They calculate that replacing the triple lock with a "smoothed earnings link" from next year could save £650 million annually by the end of the current Parliament (2029-30)

*   **Critics (Resolution Foundation, Intergenerational Foundation)**: These organizations argue the triple lock is "intergenerationally unfair" because the increasing costs fall on the current working population, while pensioners have seen greater living standards growth

*   **Supporters (Pensions Policy Institute - PPI)**: The PPI argues that the triple lock helps ensure an adequate standard of living during retirement and is important for younger generations as it maintains the "intergenerational contract" – the expectation that current workers will receive similar benefits when they retire
They suggest that adequacy would be harder to achieve if the State Pension were only increased in line with average earnings
*   The State Pension is the largest single driver of higher welfare spending in the current Parliament, projected to cost £13.8 billion more in real terms by 2029-30
*   The IFS notes that a continued commitment to the triple lock means significant pressure to adjust other parts of state spending, potentially through rising taxes or scaling back other priorities
The Intergenerational Foundation further argues that the policy increasingly shifts resources from younger, less affluent workers to older, wealthier pensioners
